So while they're having a steady decline, ours had a dramatic decline, but we're right now equivalent to the Regina Police Service. And also the Ementim Police Services are reporting significant decline as well.

There are several factors that I feel that contribute to this decline. First off is the training gap prior to 2019 information obtained from the members of the public was documented in a simple occurrence report.
Post 2019 contact interviews are a criteria-based method of information collection.

From my experience, and as a gang unit supervisor, where they utilize a criteria-based system, I know that criteria-based collection requires continual education as to the criteria and the scenarios where each criteria would be appropriate.

And to lay out when a contact interview is not required due to statutory authority or when an investigation is being conducted. So just by the fact that we've now moved from just an open-ended reporting system to a criteria-based,
there just requires that much more effort by our police service to make sure that we have continual education and that we build that continue that continuity into it.
Due to the patrol reorganization that included the addition of the patrol inspectors in creation of a new district to district boundaries,
contact interviewing was not provided to patrol division in 2022. So obviously that's something for 2023 that we'll be looking to enhance and to incorporate in 2023.
In addition, there's administrative challenges. Contact interview reporting exists as part of our Saskatoon Police Service Information Management System, which you may know is called Sims.
Our record-market management system has numerous checks and balances to ensure that our reports are secure and can be audited and tracked.
As an unexpected consequence, if members leave a contact interview and then it's reviewed and found not to be a contact interview,
there are numerous administrative steps and approvals that have to take place to have that report converted to an appropriate report and for that contact interview that would be removed.
It's our intention to review the administrative process with the intent of streamlining this process and make this much more member-friendly,
because I feel that there is some frustration with that process and that may have resulted in some of the reasons for the decline.
In addition, calls for service for contact interviews to occur requires an officer to be in a position when they're patrolling and making observations relating to the three criteria.
This can be impacted by high calls for service and low staffing is there's just less time for those patrol observations.
And then also public engagement, a willingness of the public to call police will reduce contact interviews as members are now acting on an active investigation with a complainant.

It's as simple as that to that. Instead of an observation made, we have the public to general public who trust our police service and if they see something they're going to call us and we're going to respond.
And that negates the need for contact interview.

And then finally, expectations, we should expect that there is a reduction considering we've established a very defined criteria setting out when a contact with the public should take place and more importantly when they shouldn't take place.
So actually, our expectations should be that this number should decline.
Example number, just some example. So when we consider criteria number two basically says that we can approach a person if they're doing something that's concerning.
In a lot of cases that same behavior would be concerning to the general public and it will likely generate a call from the public.
If we've seen it and we find it concerning general public, if they see it they're going to be calling us as well.
Example, another example, criteria three says that if a person looks hurt lost or a need of assistance.
If a person appears at risk and our members find that risk, then this would then be an on-view call and we would generate an occurrence report.
The contact interview would only be applicable if the person clearly shows that they don't require assistance.
So when you think about that, what did that criteria alone? We've seen something that we think this person is in need.
We've approached them. So majority of the cases, we're going to encounter that they are actually require assistance.
And we would generate, we would call an ambulance, we would have our members generate a call and we would have that contact with the public documented in other ways.
And then example number one refers to criteria one and it says if we find someone in location for no reason, they can be spoken to.
As soon as my report, this is often the scenario, I think we mentioned it in the second round 30%.
Where an officer approaches a person walking in a non-residential area, industrial park late at night, again late at night, as described most of our contacts are between 11 and 8 in the morning.
For this criteria, the matter requires our officers to be able to patrol areas that are non-populated late at night.
